clinicalPearls: A hereditary periodic fever syndrome caused by mutations in NLRP12, a regulator of inflammatory signalling
Also termed familial cold autoinflammatory syndrome type 2, reflecting cold-triggered attacks in many patients
Recurrent episodes feature fever, urticaria-like rash, arthralgia or myalgia, and headache
Cold exposure is a common but not universal trigger of flares
Some patients report sensorineural hearing loss and aphthous ulcers alongside the periodic features
Diagnosis combines a compatible clinical picture, family history, and NLRP12 genetic testing after excluding cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes
Anti-inflammatory therapy, including interleukin-1 directed treatment in selected cases, can reduce the frequency and severity of attacks
reference.pathophysiology: NLRP12 autoinflammatory syndrome is caused by mutations in NLRP12, a NOD-like receptor family member that normally acts as a negative regulator of inflammatory signalling pathways such as nuclear factor kappa B. Loss of this regulatory function permits excessive inflammatory signalling and cytokine production, producing recurrent systemic inflammation. Cold exposure can precipitate attacks, giving rise to the familial cold autoinflammatory phenotype. The episodic fevers, rash, and musculoskeletal symptoms reflect this intermittent innate immune activation, and interleukin-1 pathway involvement underlies the benefit seen with IL-1 directed therapy in some patients.
additionalDifferentials: Cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes (NLRP3, including familial cold autoinflammatory syndrome type 1)
additionalInvestigations: Cold provocation history and, where appropriate, controlled cold challenge
Audiometry if hearing loss is suspected
Skin biopsy of the rash in uncertain cases
Screening to exclude NLRP3-related cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes
redFlags: Features suggesting systemic amyloidosis from chronic inflammation
Severe or frequent disabling attacks despite treatment
Neurological symptoms warranting evaluation for alternative diagnoses
reference.prognosis: NLRP12 autoinflammatory syndrome generally has a favourable prognosis with a relapsing course; attacks are often milder than in some cryopyrinopathies and can be reduced with anti-inflammatory therapy.
pitfalls: Labelling all cold-triggered periodic fevers as NLRP3-related cryopyrinopathy
Overlooking NLRP12 when NLRP3 testing is negative in a cold-sensitive patient
Attributing episodic urticaria to chronic spontaneous urticaria alone
Failing to monitor for hearing loss and amyloidosis over time
management: Counsel on avoidance of cold exposure, the common precipitant of attacks
Treat flares symptomatically with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and short courses of corticosteroids
Use interleukin-1-targeted therapy (anakinra or canakinumab) for frequent or refractory attacks given interleukin-1 pathway involvement
Manage the urticaria-like rash, arthralgia and headache of individual episodes
Undertake audiometry to detect and monitor sensorineural hearing loss
Coordinate care through clinical immunology and rheumatology
Provide genetic counselling and family screening given autosomal dominant inheritance
